problem: Let $f(x,y,z)=\frac{9}{x+2y-z}.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(2,1,1).$

feedback.problem: Let $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Find the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\pi ).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The linear approximation of the function $f$ at the point $(a,b)$ is given by

$$
f(x,y)≈f(a,b)+∇f(a,b)\cdot ⟨x-a,y-b⟩.
$$

So, the linear approximation of $f$ at the point $(-1,\pi )$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\pi )+∇f(-1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\pi ⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

From the definition of $f,$ we have that $f(-1,\pi )=1.$ Computing the partial derivatives, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡y\, &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{x}(-1,\pi )=-1, \\ {f}_{y} & =-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y &  & ⇒\, & {f}_{y}(-1,\pi )=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the gradient of the function at the point $(-1,\pi )$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f(-1,\pi ) & =⟨-1,0⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the linear approximation of the function $f$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x,y) & ≈f(-1,\pi )+∇f(-1,\pi )\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈1+⟨-1,0⟩\cdot ⟨x+1,y-\pi ⟩ \\  & ≈1-(x+1)+0 \\  & ≈-x.\end{aligned}
$$
